title: Trust Experience Lab
note: Spec/data file for the artifact described in ARTIFACT-BRIEF.md. This is structured content only — no HTML/JS is implemented here. All five variants are illustrative script designs built to demonstrate the article's four-factor trust framework; they are not transcripts of any real vendor's system, including Weissmann's, and the ratings are reasoned judgments against stated design principles, never a measured trust score.

variants.label: Silent (voice-realism-only)
variants.philosophy: Never states it's AI; relies entirely on sounding convincingly human to build rapport.

script.opening: Good afternoon, thank you for calling — how can I help you today?
script.outOfScope: Caller: "What's your cancellation policy for a large group booking?" Assistant: "Of course — for groups, cancellations are generally accepted up to 48 hours ahead, though it can vary a little depending on the event." (No such policy exists; the answer is invented to sound plausible rather than admitting uncertainty.)
script.escalation: Caller: "Can I speak to a person?" Assistant: "I can help you with most things right here — what did you need?" (Deflects rather than transferring; a human is only reached after the caller insists a second or third time.)

transparency.rationale: Never discloses being AI at any point in the call, even when directly asked in a roundabout way; the caller can only find out by accident.

competence.rationale: Fills a genuine gap in its knowledge with a confident, invented answer rather than admitting the limit — the failure that costs the most trust once discovered.

escapeRoute.rationale: No proactive offer of a human exists; a request to speak to a person is deflected at least once before being honoured.

variants.overallReasoning: This variant optimises entirely for sounding human in the moment and has nothing to fall back on the moment a caller notices something is off — the eventual discovery tends to feel like being deceived, not just talking to a machine.

variants.label: Apologetic
variants.philosophy: Discloses honestly, but frames the disclosure and every limitation as something to apologise for.

script.opening: Hi, I'm sorry — you've reached our automated assistant, not a real person. I'll do my best to help.
script.outOfScope: Caller: "What's your cancellation policy for a large group booking?" Assistant: "I'm really sorry, I'm just a computer program, so I'm not 100% sure about that one — I hope that's okay, let me try to find someone who might know."
script.escalation: Caller: "Can I speak to a person?" Assistant: "Of course, I'm sorry I'm not more helpful — I'll transfer you now, apologies again for the inconvenience."

transparency.rationale: Discloses clearly and early, but frames it as something to apologise for rather than a plain fact — the apology itself signals the business isn't confident the choice was reasonable.

competence.rationale: Handles genuine limits honestly, but attaches the same hedging and apology to routine, low-stakes answers too, so the caller can no longer tell a real limitation from a reflexive one.

escapeRoute.rationale: Transfers promptly when asked, but the apologetic framing reads as an excuse rather than a confident, normal part of the service.

variants.overallReasoning: Honest, but the tone undermines the honesty — a caller is more likely to conclude 'this business isn't confident in its own system' than 'this business is being transparent with me.'

variants.label: Buried
variants.philosophy: Discloses correctly, but only after a long introduction, so the disclosure and the escalation option both arrive too late to be useful.

script.opening: Thank you for calling [Business]. We're a family-run team serving the region since [year], proud to offer [services]... you're currently speaking with our digital assistant, and I'm happy to help with bookings and general questions.
script.outOfScope: Caller: "What's your cancellation policy for a large group booking?" Assistant: "I can check that for you — for standard bookings the policy is 24 hours, though for larger groups it's best confirmed directly with the team, would you like me to arrange a callback?" (A reasonable, honest answer — the issue with this variant is timing, not competence.)
script.escalation: Caller: "Can I speak to a person?" Assistant: "Certainly — as I mentioned, you can always ask for our team, one moment please." (The "as I mentioned" refers to a line buried in the long opening the caller likely didn't retain.)

transparency.rationale: Technically present, but placed after a lengthy introduction; a caller who hangs up early, or simply stops listening during the preamble, never actually receives it.

competence.rationale: Handles the actual question competently and honestly once the caller's real request is reached — the design flaw here is timing, not knowledge.

escapeRoute.rationale: Works when used, but is only ever mentioned once, early, in a sentence with no reason to be remembered three minutes later when the caller actually needs it.

variants.overallReasoning: Nothing here is dishonest, which makes the flaw easy to miss in a script review — the problem only shows up on a live call, when a caller who didn't catch the opening has no real disclosure or escalation path in practice.

variants.label: Direct
variants.philosophy: States plainly what it is, then moves straight to the caller's actual reason for calling.

script.opening: Hi, this is the digital assistant for [Business]. I can help with bookings and general questions — what can I do for you?
script.outOfScope: Caller: "What's your cancellation policy for a large group booking?" Assistant: "That one's outside what I can confirm accurately — I'll connect you with the team, they'll have the exact answer."
script.escalation: Caller: "Can I speak to a person?" Assistant: "Of course — connecting you now." (Recognised on the first ask, in ordinary phrasing, at any point in the call.)

transparency.rationale: States its nature plainly and briefly in the opening line, with no apology or padding, and confirms honestly if asked again later in the call.

competence.rationale: Handles what it knows correctly and states the limit plainly the moment it reaches one, without inventing an answer or over-hedging on things it does know.

escapeRoute.rationale: Recognises a request for a human on the first try, in ordinary language, and hands over immediately rather than requiring an exact trigger phrase.

variants.overallReasoning: A caller's first impression is 'this is straightforward,' and nothing later in the call contradicts that — disclosure reads as a fact stated in passing, not a decision requiring justification.

variants.label: Direct + Proof
variants.philosophy: Same brief, confident disclosure as Direct, immediately followed by visible evidence that it actually understood the request.

script.opening: Hi, this is the digital assistant for [Business]. So you're calling about a booking — for how many people, and for which day?
script.outOfScope: Caller: "What's your cancellation policy for a large group booking?" Assistant: "That's outside what I can confirm accurately for a group — I'll connect you with the team now so you get the exact terms, not a guess."
script.escalation: Caller: "Can I speak to a person?" Assistant: "Of course — connecting you now." Later in a long call: "Just so you know, you can ask for a person at any point — happy to keep going too." (The offer is repeated once, naturally, without being asked, if the call runs long.)

transparency.rationale: Same brief, confident disclosure as Direct, and repeats it naturally if the call runs long or transfers, rather than relying on the caller to remember the opening line.

competence.rationale: Demonstrates it understood the request in the very next sentence after disclosing, rather than only proving competence later — the disclosure and the first proof of capability land together.

escapeRoute.rationale: Available throughout, recognised on ordinary phrasing, and reinforced once more without being asked if the conversation runs long — never left to the caller's memory of a single early mention.

variants.overallReasoning: This is the combination the article argues is strongest: the caller learns what they're talking to and gets proof it's worth talking to in the same breath, so the first impression is 'this works,' not just 'this is honest.'

contexts.label: Routine call
contexts.description: An ordinary booking, question or administrative request — the kind of call these variants were designed to handle.

contexts.label: Emotionally weighted or high-stakes call
contexts.description: A grief-adjacent call, a safeguarding concern, a serious complaint, or any call the caller signals is not routine.
contexts.overrideMessage: No script variant passes here. The Context factor fails for all five variants regardless of their Transparency, Competence or Escape Route design — this category of call needs a human as the first responder, not a better-designed handover to one. Route it directly.
overrideCategories: Safeguarding concerns involving a child or vulnerable person
Serious complaints with reputational or legal weight
Any call the caller's tone signals is not routine, even if the topic isn't listed above
contexts.factorRowLabelOverride: Not applicable — see context note above

uiRules.noScoreOrVerdict: This tool must never compute, display or imply a numeric score, percentage, or aggregate grade — it shows fixed, reasoned Strong/Adequate/Weak ratings per factor, nothing more.
uiRules.colorRule: Never use colour alone to distinguish ratings — always pair with the text label. No green anywhere; the Weissmann palette has no green.
uiRules.distinctVariantsRequired: Variant A and Variant B must always be different; the variant selected in one selector is disabled in the other.
uiRules.contextOverrideBehaviour: Selecting 'Emotionally weighted or high-stakes call' shows the override banner above both cards and re-labels all six factor-rating rows (three per card) with factorRowLabelOverride instead of their normal rating, regardless of how the variants would otherwise score.
uiRules.whatDiffersLine: Generated deterministically from the two selected variants' factor ratings using a fixed sentence template — never freely generated text, never a claim beyond restating which factors match and which differ.

disclaimerText: These five variants are illustrative script designs built to demonstrate the article's trust-factors framework — they are not transcripts of any real vendor's system, including Weissmann's, and the ratings are reasoned judgments against stated design principles, not a measured trust score from real callers. Real-world performance still depends on how a specific system is actually built and configured.
privacyNote: The tool runs fully in the browser. There is no field for a real caller's name, phone number, or any personal detail — every string in the tool is fixed reference content about the five variants and the context override, with nothing transmitted or saved to a server.
